Neurofibroma

LO 1–2
Benign PNS tumor · WHO Grade I ~90% solitary & sporadic Unencapsulated — infiltrates the fascicle
How boards would word it

"A 27-year-old woman presents for evaluation of a soft, painless nodule on her forearm that she first noticed 8 months ago and that has grown slowly since. On examination it is a well-circumscribed, flesh-colored subcutaneous nodule; gentle lateral pressure causes it to invaginate into an underlying dermal defect ('buttonholing'). Tapping the lesion does not reproduce tingling or pain (negative Tinel sign). She has no café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, or family history of similar skin findings. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Solitary (sporadic) neurofibroma
What to look for: the buttonholing sign (soft, compressible into a dermal defect) plus a negative Tinel sign favor neurofibroma over schwannoma, which is typically firmer, encapsulated, and Tinel-positive. The absence of café-au-lait macules or freckling argues against NF1-associated disease — about 90% of neurofibromas are solitary and sporadic, not part of a syndrome.
LO1 · Natural History
Etiology & Epidemiology

Neurofibromas are composed of neoplastic Schwann cells admixed with fibroblasts, mast cells, macrophages, and perineural cells within the nerve fascicle. Roughly 90% are solitary and sporadic, unrelated to any syndrome, typically presenting between ages 20–30 with no sex predilection.

The remainder occur in the context of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) — an autosomal dominant disorder (chromosome 17q11.2, ~50% de novo) caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NF1 tumor-suppressor gene, which encodes neurofibromin, a negative regulator of RAS/MAPK signaling. NF1 affects roughly 1 in 2,500–3,000 people, and more than 95% of affected individuals eventually develop cutaneous neurofibromas. Multiple neurofibromas are virtually diagnostic of NF1 — a single lesion is not.

Pathology & Pathophysiology

Tumor formation requires biallelic NF1 inactivation ("second hit") in the Schwann cell lineage:

Biallelic NF1 loss
→
↓ Neurofibromin
→
Constitutive RAS-GTP
→
MAPK / PI3K-AKT signaling
→
Schwann cell proliferation + stromal recruitment

Unlike schwannomas, neurofibromas are unencapsulated and infiltrate diffusely between nerve fascicles. Histology shows uniformly distributed, comma-shaped spindle cells in a myxoid, collagen-rich matrix; spindle cells are S100-positive, with entrapped axons positive for neurofilament. Progesterone receptors are expressed on ~75% of neurofibromas, thought to explain accelerated growth during puberty and pregnancy.

Localized

  • ~90% of neurofibromas
  • Solitary, superficial cutaneous nerves
  • Slow-growing, usually <5 cm
  • Not associated with NF1

Diffuse

  • Children & young adults
  • Subcutaneous tissue, head/neck
  • Plaque-like skin thickening
  • Usually solitary, not NF1

Plexiform

  • Diffuse — a long nerve segment + branches, beyond the epineurium
  • Pathognomonic for NF1
  • Usually congenital / early childhood
  • Significant malignant potential
Gross pathology — plexiform neurofibroma (arrows) diffusely expanding a nerve trunk along its fascicles, with normal-caliber nerve in between.
Prognosis if Untreated

Solitary and diffuse neurofibromas essentially never transform malignantly. Plexiform neurofibromas carry the meaningful risk: roughly a 2–13% per-lesion risk, and an estimated 15.8% lifetime risk, of transformation to a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST) — the leading cause of premature death in NF1, which itself reduces life expectancy by 8–15 years. Persistent pain, rapid growth, or a change in texture of an existing plexiform lesion are the classic warning signs of transformation.

LO2 · Typical Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Cutaneous neurofibromas typically emerge in late childhood to adolescence and increase steadily in number with age — from a few lesions to, in heavily affected NF1 patients, thousands covering the skin. They present as soft, flesh-colored to violaceous papules and nodules that can be gently pushed into an underlying dermal defect with a fingertip (the "buttonholing" sign). Symptoms include intermittent pruritus, stinging, or pain, though many are asymptomatic aside from cosmetic concern.

Clinical comparison — cutaneous (fleshy/pedunculated), subcutaneous (firm, ± tender nodules), and plexiform ("bag of worms") neurofibromas.

Cutaneous

  • Soft, flesh-colored papules/nodules
  • Positive buttonholing sign
  • Pruritus, stinging, or pain
  • No neurologic deficit

Subcutaneous

  • Firm nodules along a peripheral nerve
  • Tender / painful
  • Can cause neurologic deficits
  • Slightly higher malignant potential

Plexiform

  • "Bag of worms" (diffuse) or "beads on a string" (nodular)
  • Overlying hyperpigmentation, hypertrophy, hypertrichosis
  • Congenital/early childhood (diffuse) vs. later (nodular)
  • Can compress vital structures → focal deficits
Multiple discrete cutaneous neurofibromas on the trunk — this burden of lesions is pathognomonic for NF1 (von Recklinghausen disease); a single lesion is not.
When to suspect NF1

Multiple neurofibromas + ≥6 café-au-lait macules (>5 mm prepubertal / >15 mm postpubertal) + axillary/inguinal freckling + Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas) → think NF1. Full diagnostic criteria and management are covered on the Neurofibromatosis tab.

Café-au-lait macules — smooth, "coast of California" borders (NF1) vs. the jagged, "coast of Maine" borders seen in McCune-Albright syndrome.
Pearl

Neurofibroma vs. schwannoma: a neurofibroma is unencapsulated and infiltrates between nerve fascicles, so it can't be shelled out without sacrificing the nerve, and Tinel's sign is inconsistent. A schwannoma is encapsulated and eccentric to the nerve, so it can usually be enucleated with the nerve preserved, and is more reliably Tinel-positive on palpation. (See the Schwannoma tab.)

Neurofibromatosis

LO 1–2
Phakomatosis (neurocutaneous syndrome) NF1 → PNS phenotype NF2 → CNS phenotype
How boards would word it — NF1

"A 6-year-old boy is brought in for evaluation of light-brown skin patches present since infancy and several new, soft, painless bumps on his trunk that have appeared over the past year. Examination reveals eight hyperpigmented macules, the largest 2 cm, and freckling in both axillae. Slit-lamp exam shows pigmented iris nodules bilaterally. His father has similar skin findings. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (von Recklinghausen disease)
What to look for: ≥6 café-au-lait macules (>5 mm prepubertal) + axillary freckling + Lisch nodules + an affected first-degree relative together satisfy the diagnostic pattern for NF1. Note the age-dependent sequence — café-au-lait spots and Lisch nodules typically precede the cutaneous neurofibromas themselves, which are only just emerging here.
How boards would word it — NF2

"A 22-year-old woman presents with progressive bilateral hearing loss and tinnitus over the past year, with intermittent vertigo. She was diagnosed with bilateral cataracts at age 19. MRI of the brain with contrast reveals bilateral masses at the internal auditory canals. Her maternal aunt has a similar history. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Neurofibromatosis type 2
What to look for: bilateral vestibular schwannomas is the key finding — a unilateral internal-auditory-canal mass in an older adult would instead favor a sporadic schwannoma (see the Schwannoma tab). Early-onset bilateral cataracts and a family history seal it. NF2 is a CNS-predominant disease (merlin, chromosome 22) — distinct from NF1's peripheral/cutaneous phenotype (neurofibromin, chromosome 17).
▶
▶ Neurofibromatosis Type 1 & 2: Symptoms, Diagnosis & Management | High-Yield Clinical Review
Video — "Neurofibromatosis Type 1 & 2: Symptoms, Diagnosis & Management | High-Yield Clinical Review" (YouTube)
LO1 · Natural History
Etiology & Epidemiology

Neurofibromatosis belongs to the phakomatoses — neurocutaneous syndromes of ectodermal-tissue origin featuring disseminated glial hamartomas ("phakomas"). Other family members include tuberous sclerosis, von Hippel–Lindau disease, and Sturge-Weber syndrome.

NF1 (von Recklinghausen disease) is an autosomal dominant disorder — about half of cases are familial, half are new (de novo) mutations — with nearly complete penetrance by age 5, though clinical severity is highly variable. It is the most common genetic disorder affecting the nervous system, with an incidence around 1:2,500–3,000.

NF2 is much rarer, roughly 1:33,000–50,000, also autosomal dominant. A third entity, schwannomatosis (mutation in SMARCB1, chromosome 22), presents mainly with pain along a specific nerve rather than the classic NF1/NF2 tumor pattern.

Pathophysiology
NF1 gene mutation (chr 17)
→
↓ Neurofibromin (RAS-GAP)
→
Unchecked RAS-GTP signaling
→
Uninhibited Schwann/neural-crest cell growth
NF2 gene mutation (chr 22)
→
↓ Merlin (schwannomin)
→
Loss of cytoskeletal tumor-suppression
→
Schwann cell / meningeal / ependymal proliferation
NF1NF2
Gene / chromosomeNF1, 17q11.2NF2, 22q12
ProteinNeurofibromin (RAS-GAP)Merlin / schwannomin (cytoskeletal)
Incidence~1:2,500–3,000~1:33,000–50,000
Predominant systemPeripheral (PNS) — skin, peripheral nervesCentral (CNS) — vestibulocochlear nerve, meninges, cord
Prognosis if Untreated

Most NF-associated tumors are benign, but malignant transformation occurs in a meaningful minority (roughly <5–10% of NF1 tumors, e.g., transformation of a plexiform neurofibroma to MPNST — see the Neurofibroma tab). Mortality is increased relative to the general population, with average life expectancy around 60 years in NF1 and 40 years in NF2, driven largely by tumor burden and malignant transformation.

LO2 · Typical Clinical Presentation
Presentation

NF1 follows a classic age-dependent sequence: café-au-lait macules are often present at birth or in infancy (before age 2), axillary/inguinal freckling and Lisch nodules emerge in early childhood (ages 3–10), and cutaneous neurofibromas appear in adolescence and increase in number with age. Presentation ranges from mild to severe. NF2 has a later typical onset (18–24 years) and is dominated by CNS/eighth-nerve tumors rather than skin findings.

NF1 (left) — associated tumors and melanocyte-dysfunction features — vs. NF2 (right) — early-onset cataract and CNS/eighth-nerve tumor pattern.
Mnemonic — NF1

"CAFE SPOTS": Café-au-lait spots, Axillary freckling, neuroFibromas, nodules in the Eye (Lisch), Skeletal abnormalities (e.g., scoliosis), high blood Pressure, Optic tumor, Thin/short Stature.

Skin & pigmentation (NF1)

  • ≥6 café-au-lait macules (>5 mm prepubertal / >15 mm postpubertal), onset before age 2
  • Axillary & inguinal freckling (age 3–5)
  • Cutaneous/subcutaneous/plexiform neurofibromas — onset adolescence, malignant transformation possible

Ocular (NF1)

  • Lisch nodules — pigmented iris hamartomas, age 5–10, seen in the vast majority of NF1 patients
  • Optic pathway glioma — unilateral vision loss, proptosis, or precocious puberty

Skeletal (NF1)

  • Scoliosis, sphenoid wing dysplasia
  • Cortical thinning, fractures, pseudoarthrosis (esp. tibia)
  • Short stature
(a,b) Multiple neurofibromas of varying size in the axilla/trunk. (c,d) Café-au-lait macules >15 mm with irregular borders on the hand and thigh.
Trunk of a 35-year-old woman — four café-au-lait spots plus scattered neurofibroma papules/nodules.

A photo of multiple discrete cutaneous neurofibromas on the back/neck — the same lesion pattern discussed above — is shown on the Neurofibroma tab.

Skeletal involvement in NF1 — inspect the back/shoulders for asymmetry from scoliosis or other bone dysplasia.
Lisch nodules — right eyes of a father and son, both with NF1 (illustrates the autosomal dominant, familial pattern).
Lisch nodules close-up — multiple well-defined, brown-yellow iris hamartomas.
NF2 presentation
  • Bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) at the internal acoustic meatus → tinnitus, hearing loss, vertigo — virtually diagnostic (unilateral favors sporadic schwannoma instead)
  • Early-onset bilateral cataracts
  • Multiple CNS tumors — meningiomas, spinal ependymomas
  • Other, nonspecific: seizures, skin nodules (schwannomas), café-au-lait spots
Pearl

NF2 mnemonic: mutation on chromosome 22 ("Twenty-2"), and the hallmark findings — schwannomas and cataracts — manifest on 2 sides.

Schwannoma

LO 1–2
Benign PNS tumor · WHO Grade I Most common: CN VIII (acoustic neuroma) Encapsulated — eccentric to the nerve
How boards would word it

"A 54-year-old man presents with several months of progressive hearing loss in his right ear accompanied by ringing and intermittent unsteadiness. Weber test lateralizes to the left ear, and audiometry confirms sensorineural hearing loss on the right, worse at higher frequencies. Examination also reveals decreased sensation over the right cheek and a diminished right corneal reflex. Contrast-enhanced MRI shows a well-circumscribed, homogeneously enhancing mass in the right internal auditory canal extending into the cerebellopontine angle. There is no family history of similar tumors, and no skin or ocular findings are noted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)
What to look for: unilateral sensorineural hearing loss + tinnitus (CN VIII) progressing to ipsilateral trigeminal findings (CN V — cheek numbness, diminished corneal reflex) as the tumor enlarges into the cerebellopontine angle is the classic sequence. Unilateral involvement with no family history favors a sporadic schwannoma; bilateral disease would instead point to NF2 (see the Neurofibromatosis tab).
LO1 · Natural History
Etiology & Epidemiology

Schwannomas are benign, generally solitary and sporadic peripheral-nerve-sheath tumors arising from Schwann cells; they can arise from any cranial or spinal nerve except CN I and II. They account for 6–8% of all primary intracranial tumors and typically present in the 4th–6th decade of life.

The eighth cranial nerve (vestibular) is the single most common site — the resulting tumor is the vestibular schwannoma, also called an acoustic neuroma, and is the most common tumor of the cerebellopontine angle. The trigeminal (CN V) nerve is the second most common site. For vestibular schwannoma specifically: median age ~52, incidence ~4:100,000/year, no sex predilection. Most are unilateral — bilateral acoustic neuromas are strongly associated with neurofibromatosis type 2 (see the Neurofibromatosis tab), which also greatly increases overall schwannoma incidence.

Pathology & Pathophysiology

Schwannomas are well-encapsulated and grow eccentric to their nerve of origin — the opposite of a neurofibroma, which is unencapsulated and infiltrates the fascicle (see the Neurofibroma tab pearl). Grossly they are firm, encapsulated masses. Microscopically they show spindle-shaped Schwann cells, axons, macrophages, T-cells, fibroblasts, blood vessels, and extracellular matrix, classically arranged in alternating Antoni A (compact spindle cells in palisades) and Antoni B (myxoid, hypocellular) zones; cells are S-100 positive.

NF2 gene inactivation (chr 22)
→
↓ Merlin expression
→
Failure of normal post-injury nerve repair
→
Encapsulated schwannoma

A rare malignant counterpart exists — variably termed malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor, malignant schwannoma, or neurofibrosarcoma.

Origin and growth — the tumor arises on the vestibular portion of CN VIII within the internal auditory canal, expanding to abut the facial nerve before extending toward the cerebellopontine angle.
Contrast MRI — a well-circumscribed, avidly enhancing mass at the cerebellopontine angle/internal auditory canal (arrow), typical imaging appearance of a vestibular schwannoma.
T1-weighted post-contrast MRI, axial and coronal views — a right-sided cerebellopontine-angle mass extending into the internal auditory canal (porus acousticus), with strong peripheral enhancement and a hypointense center suggesting necrosis.
Prognosis if Untreated

Overall prognosis is favorable — schwannomas are WHO grade I, slow-growing, benign tumors. Left untreated, however, progressive growth can worsen cranial neuropathies and, via mass effect on the cerebellopontine angle, cause ataxia (cerebellar compression) or hydrocephalus (4th ventricle compression).

LO2 · Typical Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Presentation reflects a mass effect that depends on tumor location and size. Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) is by far the most common presentation, following a two-stage pattern as the tumor grows from the internal auditory canal into the cerebellopontine angle.

Early — internal auditory canal

  • Cochlear nerve: unilateral sensorineural hearing loss (most common symptom; acute onset in up to 10%), tinnitus
  • Vestibular nerve: dizziness, unsteady gait/disequilibrium — may be absent or occur late

Late — cerebellopontine angle

  • CN V: facial paresthesia/hypoesthesia, unilateral facial pain
  • CN VII: unilateral facial weakness → can progress to paralysis (accompanies hearing loss in >50% of patients)
  • Cerebellum: ataxia
  • 4th ventricle: hydrocephalus
Structure-related symptoms of compression, by nerve/structure — vestibular (vertigo), cochlear (hearing loss, tinnitus), facial (weakness), trigeminal (facial pain), cerebellum (ataxia).
Pearl

Solitary, unilateral schwannoma is the typical sporadic presentation covered here. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are NF2 until proven otherwise (see the Neurofibromatosis tab) — and remember the Neurofibroma-tab pearl: schwannomas are encapsulated/eccentric and more reliably Tinel-positive, whereas neurofibromas are unencapsulated and infiltrate the fascicle.

Neuroblastoma

LO 1–2
Malignant · neural crest origin Most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood Mean age at diagnosis 1–2 yr
How boards would word it

"An 18-month-old girl is brought in for evaluation of a firm, irregular abdominal mass that crosses the midline, noted incidentally on exam. Over the past month she has had decreased appetite and mild weight loss. Blood pressure is elevated for age, and there is bilateral periorbital bruising. Urine studies show markedly elevated homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Neuroblastoma
What to look for: age <2, an abdominal mass that crosses the midline (the key distractor is Wilms tumor/nephroblastoma, which is classically smooth and does not cross the midline), periorbital ecchymoses ("raccoon eyes" — orbital metastasis), and elevated catecholamine metabolites (HVA/VMA) together clinch neuroblastoma over other pediatric abdominal masses.
LO1 · Natural History
Etiology & Epidemiology

Neuroblastoma is a malignant, embryonal neuroendocrine neoplasm of the sympathetic nervous system arising from neural crest cells. It is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children and the most common malignancy diagnosed in infants — the third most common childhood cancer overall (behind leukemia and brain tumors), accounting for ~8% of childhood malignancies (~500 cases/year in the US). Mean age at diagnosis is 1–2 years, and most children have already progressed to advanced-stage disease by the time they're diagnosed.

Cause is unclear. Genetic associations include chromosomal deletions (1p, 11q, 14q — found in ~50% of cases) and amplification/overexpression of the MYCN (N-myc) oncogene, a marker of poor prognosis; germline gain-of-function ALK mutations and high-risk-associated LIN28B polymorphisms are also frequently implicated. Risk factors include maternal gestational diabetes, opiate use, and folate deficiency, plus congenital syndromes — Turner syndrome, neurofibromatosis, Hirschsprung disease, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome — and familial cases.

Typical origin — a paraspinal/adrenal tumor arising from sympathetic neural crest tissue adjacent to the spinal nerves, distinct from the adjacent kidney.
Pathology & Pathophysiology
Neural crest cell
→
Chromosomal deletions (1p/11q/14q), MYCN amplification, ALK mutation
→
Malignant transformation of sympathetic precursor
→
Tumor of adrenal medulla / sympathetic chain, with metastatic potential

Tumor cells derive from neural crest precursors destined to become adrenal medullary chromaffin cells and sympathetic neurons, so tumors can arise anywhere sympathetic tissue is found: the adrenal medulla (~47%, the majority), the retroperitoneal sympathetic chain (~24%), and elsewhere along the paravertebral ganglia and paraganglia (e.g., carotid body).

Histologically: small round blue cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, bombesin- and NSE-positive, classically forming Homer Wright rosettes — halo-like clusters of neuroblasts surrounding a central pale core of neuropil (also seen in medulloblastoma and other primitive neuroectodermal tumors). Calcification is often visible on imaging. The most common site of metastasis is the long bones.

Neuroblastoma arises when neural crest cells mature improperly and form tumors along the sympathetic chain — adrenal medulla, neck, chest, abdomen, or near the spine.
Histology — small round blue cells with hyperchromatic nuclei clustering into rosette-like groups, consistent with Homer Wright rosettes.
CT abdomen with contrast — a large, heterogeneous right adrenal mass with little vascular enhancement, a common imaging appearance of adrenal neuroblastoma (calcification is common, though not seen here).
Prognosis if Untreated

Prognosis depends heavily on tumor biology and stage: younger age and lower stage favor a better outcome, while MYCN amplification confers a poor prognosis regardless of other factors. Remarkably, neuroblastoma is one of the few malignancies capable of spontaneous regression even in metastatic disease — classically in infants <12 months with a localized primary tumor that has disseminated only to skin, liver, or bone marrow ("Stage 4S"), which behaves more favorably than other stage 4 disease. Without treatment, though, most children present with — and progress toward — advanced-stage disease.

LO2 · Typical Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Signs and symptoms reflect mass effect at the primary site, catecholamine secretion, and metastatic spread. General findings include failure to thrive/weight loss, fever, nausea/vomiting/anorexia, and hypertension.

Primary tumor siteAssociated signs & symptoms
Abdomen (>60% of cases)Firm, irregular mass that may cross the midline (vs. nephroblastoma/Wilms tumor, which is smooth and usually does not cross the midline); abdominal distension/pain, hepatomegaly, constipation
Chest (~20%, paravertebral ganglia)Spinal cord compression (back pain, weakness, numbness, ataxia, bowel/bladder dysfunction), scoliosis, dyspnea/cough, inspiratory stridor
NeckHorner syndrome; symptoms of spinal cord compression
Site of metastasisAssociated signs & symptoms
OrbitPeriorbital ecchymoses ("raccoon eyes"), proptosis
BoneBone pain, anemia (marrow suppression)
SkinSubcutaneous nodules
Initial, nonspecific symptoms (abdominal distension, fatigue, malaise, weight loss) progress to signs of catecholamine excess and metastatic spread (sweating, tachycardia, periorbital bruising, bone pain) as the tumor advances.
Paraneoplastic syndromes
  • Chronic diarrhea (VIP secretion) → electrolyte imbalances
  • Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia ("dancing eyes, dancing feet") — rapid, multidirectional eye movements, rhythmic limb jerks, and ataxia; etiology unclear
  • Catecholamine-related: hypertension, tachycardia, palpitations, sweating, flushing (though hypertension is more classically associated with pheochromocytoma)
Pearl — Neuroblastoma vs. Wilms tumor

Both present as a pediatric abdominal mass, but the pattern differs: neuroblastoma is irregular and crosses the midline, arises from sympathetic/neural crest tissue, and is associated with elevated HVA/VMA and (rarely) opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia. Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is a renal tumor that is typically smooth and does not cross the midline.
